title: Assess the setting before proposing the service
focus: Schools, nurseries, healthcare settings and workplace canteens have different users, facilities and approval requirements. Start with a detailed operational brief rather than an event menu. Define meal volumes, service days, dietary needs and the documentation your organisation requires. The proposed culinary partner and site arrangements must be assessed against that brief before any commitment. A clear specification gives procurement and operations a shared basis for reviewing suitability, responsibilities and the commercial proposal.

sections.title: Write a specification your teams can use
paragraphs: An institutional catering brief should be practical enough for procurement, facilities and the proposed culinary partner to review together. Record the expected meals for each sitting, operating days and location of preparation. Explain whether the organisation requires delivered food, staff at a service counter or responsibility for a complete kitchen operation.

Name the contacts who approve menus, confirm orders and receive the service. If the site has seasonal closures, changing occupancy or several buildings, include those details early. They influence staffing and transport as well as the amount of food. A timetable of actual meal windows is more useful than a daily total alone.

Keep the specification as the shared reference during discussions. When an assumption changes, update the affected menu, equipment or staffing requirement before comparing quotations. This gives the organisation a consistent basis for assessing the proposed service and makes responsibilities easier to explain to the people managing it each day.

sections.title: Agree how dietary information moves through the service
paragraphs: The organisation should provide its current dietary requirements through an agreed contact. Explain how information is approved, updated and passed to the kitchen, while following the site approach to personal information. The menu cycle, ingredient information and meal identification should use a consistent version so staff are working from the same instructions.

Requirements differ by setting. A nursery may have age-group preparation instructions, a school its own food policy, and a hospital clinically approved meal specifications. The proposed provider needs to assess the relevant requirements directly. No general menu or label can substitute for that assessment or for specialist approval where it is required.

sections.title: Evaluate the full operating cost
paragraphs: Compare proposals against the same meal volumes, service hours and responsibilities. Identify who supplies equipment, utilities, transport, service staff and clearance. An attractive meal price is only meaningful when procurement understands the work included and what the organisation must arrange separately.

Review how the agreement handles changes in demand, closures, menu substitutions and additional service periods. The written terms should explain invoicing, payment and any review points. A clear cost structure allows the organisation to budget for the whole operation and assess future changes without reopening every part of the original brief.

sections.title: Set a review rhythm from the beginning
paragraphs: Before launch, agree how the service will be reviewed and who attends those discussions. Useful measures include meal uptake, portion feedback, delivery performance and the time required to serve each sitting. The purpose is to identify practical improvements while keeping the agreed food and service requirements clear.

A short, documented review after the introduction period gives both teams a shared record of what needs attention. Confirm who will act, when a change will take effect and whether it affects the scope or price. Regular communication makes a recurring arrangement easier to manage as the organisation changes.
